To communicate means to share or exchange information, ideas, feelings, or messages with someone — in a way that the other person actually receives and understands it.

Notice there are two parts to this:

  • Sending — you put something out: a thought, a fact, an emotion, an instruction.
  • Receiving — the other person gets it and understands it.

This is the most important thing to grasp from the start: communication is not just the act of speaking or writing. It is complete only when meaning successfully travels from one person to another. If you speak but nobody understands, that is an attempt to communicate, not communication in its fullest sense.
What Can Be Communicated?

Almost anything that can be understood by another person:

  • Facts or information — "The nurse communicated the test results to the doctor."
  • Feelings or emotions — "Her tears communicated deep sadness."
  • Ideas or opinions — "The speech communicated a powerful belief in equality."
  • Instructions or decisions — "The manager communicated the new policy to the staff."
  • Needs or desires — "A baby communicates hunger by crying."

The word is broad. It does not matter what the content is — as long as you are sending meaning to someone, you are communicating.
Two Main Ways to Use It in a Sentence

1. When you name what is being shared (transitive):

Here, "communicate" takes a direct object — the thing being shared.

  • "She communicated her concerns to the board."
  • "He struggled to communicate his feelings."
  • "The sculpture communicates loneliness in a striking way."

2. When you don't name the thing (intransitive):

Here, you just describe the act of being in contact or exchanging messages with someone.

  • "The two teams need to communicate more often."
  • "They haven't communicated in years."
  • "People who communicate openly tend to have stronger relationships."
The Prepositions That Go With It

The preposition you pair with "communicate" changes the meaning slightly, so it is worth learning each one.

communicate WITH someone — the most natural and common. It suggests a two-way exchange where both sides are involved.

"She communicates with her clients every week."

communicate TO someone — more one-directional. You are delivering or sending something toward them; they are the receiver.

"The decision was communicated to all employees."

communicate THROUGH something — names the channel or method used.

"During the war, they communicated through coded letters."

communicate VIA something — same idea as "through," and slightly more formal.

"The team communicates via a shared messaging app."
Communication Does Not Require Words

This is one of the richest and most important aspects of the word. "Communicate" covers any method by which meaning passes from one to another — not just speech or writing.

  • Body language communicates. Crossed arms communicate defensiveness or discomfort. A smile communicates warmth.
  • Silence communicates. If someone asks a question and you say nothing, that silence communicates something — refusal, discomfort, or disapproval.
  • Art and music communicate. A painting can communicate grief. A song can communicate joy without a single spoken word.
  • Actions communicate. Showing up for a friend in a difficult moment communicates care and loyalty far more powerfully than words can.

So whenever you use the word "communicate," remember it is not limited to language. It covers the full range of ways in which meaning can travel between people.
How Well or Poorly Something Is Communicated

"Communicate" by itself is neutral — it does not tell you whether the communication was good or bad. You need a modifier for that:

  • "She communicated clearly." — the message was easy to understand.
  • "He communicated poorly." — the message was confusing or incomplete.
  • "They communicated openly and honestly." — nothing was hidden.
  • "The memo failed to communicate the urgency of the situation." — the communication was unsuccessful.

This means the word is flexible. You can use it to describe excellent communication or terrible communication, depending on what you add to it.
Common and Useful Patterns

Here are patterns you will see and use often:

  • communicate something to someone — "Please communicate your decision to us as soon as possible."
  • communicate with someone — "Do you communicate with your old colleagues?"
  • communicate in [form] — "He finds it easier to communicate in writing than in speech."
  • communicate a sense of [feeling/idea] — "The film communicates a deep sense of loss." (This is a very useful pattern when talking about art, literature, or creative work.)
  • find it hard/difficult to communicate — "She finds it difficult to communicate when she is upset."
  • communicate effectively — used especially in professional and academic settings to mean communicating in a way that is clear, precise, and well-understood.
Formal or Everyday?

"Communicate" works in both formal writing and everyday conversation, but it leans slightly toward the formal end. In casual speech, people often say "tell," "talk to," "message," "reach out," or "let someone know" instead.

  • Casual: "Just tell me what you need."
  • Formal: "Please communicate your requirements in writing."

Both are correct. The choice depends on the situation. In professional, academic, or analytical contexts, "communicate" is the sharper and more precise word.
Communicate vs. Similar Words — What Makes It Different?

It is easy to confuse "communicate" with words like say, tell, speak, or talk. Here is how they differ:

  • Say and tell focus on the content of spoken words. They are about what was actually said.
  • Speak and talk focus on the physical act of using your voice or having a conversation.
  • Communicate focuses on the transfer of meaning — regardless of the method.

This leads to an important real-world distinction:

You can talk a great deal without actually communicating — if the meaning never reaches the other person clearly.
You can communicate without saying a single word — through a gesture, a letter, a piece of music, or even your silence.

This is why "communicate" is a more powerful and precise word. It captures the purpose and result of the exchange, not just the surface act.
A Final Summary

Communicate means: to share meaning — whether it is a fact, a feeling, an idea, or an instruction — with one or more people, through any channel, in any form, in a way that (ideally) reaches and is understood by the other person.

It is about connection through meaning. Every time a human being successfully makes another human being understand something — through words, actions, art, expression, or silence — that is communication happening.
